s: The Ionic School of epic poetry was dominated by the Homeric tradition but avoided directly cultivating the subjects treated by Homer. Its poets developed legends about Troy, Thebes, the origins of the world, and the wars of heaven.

l: Homer, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: Homer’s poems were treated as the central works around which the later Cyclic poems were written. The text places Homer and the Homeric poems before the authors and dated works of the Cyclic poets.

l: Homeric tradition, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: The Homeric tradition shaped the style and methods of the Ionic poets. It also led those poets to choose legends beyond the range of the Iliad and Odyssey.

l: Iliad, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: The Iliad supplied the central portion of the Trojan story, while later poems treated events before and after its action. The Cyclic poets avoided trespassing on ground already occupied by the Iliad.

l: Odyssey, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: The Odyssey supplied the later central portion of the Trojan narrative, but left untold events concerning Ithaca and the ultimate fate of Odysseus. The Returns brought the general story up to the beginning of the Odyssey, and the Telegony continued it afterward.

l: Trojan story, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: Various Ionic poets gradually built up a body of epic poetry covering the whole Trojan story. The story was expanded backward through the Cyprian Lays and forward through several poems ending with the death of Odysseus.

l: Thebes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: Thebes was the subject of a separate group of epics known as the Theban Cycle. These poems treated Oedipus, the expedition of Polyneices and his allies, and the later sack of the city by the Epigoni.

l: Epic Cycle, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: The Cycle was a collection of epic poems arranged in chronological order in the Alexandrian Age, apparently by Zenodotus of Ephesus. Its poems formed an epic history of the Greek world down to the death of Odysseus.

l: Arctinus of Miletus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: Arctinus of Miletus, said to have flourished in the first Olympiad, was credited with the Aethiopis and the Sack of Ilium. He continued the Trojan story after the close of the Iliad, including the deaths of Penthesilea, Memnon, and Achilles, and he treated the sack of Troy.

l: Trojan Cycle, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: The Trojan Cycle connected the events before and after the Iliad and Odyssey through the Cyprian Lays, Aethiopis, Little Iliad, Sack of Troy, Returns, and Telegony, together with the Homeric poems. Its surviving evidence is chiefly fragments and Proclus’s abridgment preserved by Photius.

l: Cyprian Lays, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: The Cyprian Lays, attributed to Stasinus of Cyprus or Hegesinus of Salamis, treated the causes and opening events of the Trojan War. They began with Zeus’s purpose to relieve the earth, the apple of discord, and the rape of Helen, and continued to the quarrel between Achilles and Agamemnon.

l: The Aethiopis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: The Aethiopis, attributed to Arctinus of Miletus, narrated events after the death of Hector. It included the arrival and deaths of Penthesilea and Memnon, the death of Achilles, and the dispute between Odysseus and Aias over Achilles’ arms.

l: The Little Iliad, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: The Little Iliad by Lesches or Lescheos elaborated material associated with the Sack of Troy. It included the adjudgment of Achilles’ arms to Odysseus, the madness of Aias, the recovery of Philoctetes, the arrival of Neoptolemus, the making of the wooden horse, and the theft of the Palladium.

l: The Sack of Ilium, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: The Sack of Troy, also called the Sack of Ilium and attributed to Arctinus, described the wooden horse, Laocoon, Sinon, the Greek return from Tenedos, the sack and burning of Troy, and the division of the spoils. Its account was described as similar to Vergil’s version in Aeneid II.

l: Returns, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: The Returns, a five-book poem attributed to Agias or Hegias of Troezen, began after the Sack of Troy. It described the disputes and departures of the Greek heroes, the death of Agamemnon and vengeance of Orestes, and ended with Menelaus’s return home before the Odyssey.

l: The Telegony, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: The Telegony, a two-book poem by Eugammon of Cyrene, continued the story after the Odyssey. It described Odysseus’s adventures in Thesprotis, his return to Ithaca, his death at the hands of Telegonus, and the marriages of the surviving characters.

l: Odysseus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: Odysseus was the one prominent Greek hero whose adventures were not fully covered in the Returns because they were treated in the Odyssey. The Telegony related his later adventures, return to Ithaca, and death at the hands of his son Telegonus.

l: Achilles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: Achilles was a central heroic figure in the Iliad and was used as a model for the treatment of Antilochus in the Aethiopis. The Aethiopis also narrated his death by Paris’s arrow and the subsequent dispute over his arms.

l: Hesiod, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: Hesiod’s Theogony was used as a point of comparison for the account of the Titan War in the Titanomachy. His influence was also clear in the Homeric Hymns, and the Contest of Homer and Hesiod treated their dates, poetry, contest, and legendary lives.

l: Homeric Hymns, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: The Homeric Hymns are a collection of thirty-three poems regarded as the last considerable work of the Epic School and generally later than the Cyclic poems. They combine Homeric and Hesiodic influences and include longer narrative works about Demeter, Apollo, Hermes, Aphrodite, Dionysus, and Pan, as well as shorter hymns.

l: Trojan War, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: The Trojan War was treated across the Cyclic poems from its first causes through the gathering of the Achaeans, the fighting around Troy, the city’s sack, and the heroes’ returns. The enlarged narrative ended with the later fate of Odysseus in the Telegony.
